extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners / patent examiners / Office personnel evaluating obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for conducting and articulating obviousness rejections under 35 U.S.C. §103 (post-KSR), including enumerated rationales and the specific factual findings Office personnel must make to support those rationales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale D: Applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a known technique to a known device (method, or product) ready for improvement to yield predictable results;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rationale supports an obviousness rejection when a known technique is applied to a known device that is ready for improvement and the result would have been predictable to one of ordinary skill in the art. Any use of this rationale must be supported by the necessary factual findings (see general requirement to resolve the Graham inquiries and articulate findings linking facts to the legal conclusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale E: 'Obvious to try' with reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: “Obvious to try” – choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions, with a reasonable expectation of success;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May support obviousness when the problem has a finite number of identified predictable solutions and one of ordinary skill would have had a reasonable expectation of success. Do not rely on a bare 'obvious to try' assertion without showing predictability and expectation of success. Examples and case law illustrate when this does and does not apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale F: Predictable cross-field variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Known work in one field of endeavor may prompt variations of it for use in either the same field or a different one based on design incentives or other market forces if the variations are predictable to one of ordinary skill in the art;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prior-art teaching in one field can motivate predictable adaptations in the same or other fields; examiner must show that the variations would have been predictable to a person of ordinary skill. Consider analogous art guidance and reasonable pertinence to the problem addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale G: Teaching, suggestion, or motivation to modify or combine prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify the prior art reference or to combine prior art reference teachings to arrive at the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This captures the classical TSM concept: examiners should point to teaching/suggestion/motivation (explicit or implicit, including marketplace incentives or common sense) that would have led one of ordinary skill to the claimed combination. The rationale must be tied to factual findings and cannot be merely conclusory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining prior art elements to yield predictable results (rationale A)
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim based on this rationale, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries. Then, Office personnel must articulate: (1) a finding that the prior art included each element claimed, although not necessarily in a single prior art reference; (2) a finding that one of ordinary skill could have combined the elements as claimed by known methods, and each element merely performs the same function as it does separately; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill would have recognized that the results of the combination were predictable; and (4) whatever additional findings based on the Graham factual inquiries may be necessary to explain a conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All four findings must be made to support a combination-based obviousness rejection. Examiners must articulate why a person of ordinary skill would have combined the elements and why the combination would produce predictable results. Anti-patterns: pointing only to the presence of elements in prior art without finding predictability; failing to address teaching away or lack of motivation. Examples: Anderson’s-Black Rock (combination yielded no new function) vs. Adams (predictability absent because prior art taught away).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple substitution of one known element for another (rationale B)
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim based on this rationale, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries. Then, Office personnel must articulate: (1) a finding that the prior art contained a device differing from the claimed device by substitution of some components; (2) a finding that the substituted components and their functions were known in the art; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill could have substituted one known element for another and the results would have been predictable; and (4) whatever additional Graham-based findings are necessary to explain obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used when the claimed invention is a predictable result of replacing one known element with an equivalent known element. Must show the substitution would have been within the ordinary skill and predictable. Examples: In re Fout, In re O’Farrell, Ex parte Smith. Do not treat mere possibility to substitute as sufficient without predictability and supporting factual findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve the Graham factual inquiries before applying rationales
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries before applying any of the enumerated rationales for obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Graham inquiries (scope and content of the prior art; differences between the prior art and the claims; level of ordinary skill in the art; and secondary considerations) are foundational. Every rationale applied (combination, substitution, obvious-to-try, etc.) requires that these factual inquiries be addressed and that additional relevant findings be articulated where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link factual findings to the legal conclusion; avoid conclusory rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Any rationale employed must provide a link between the factual findings and the legal conclusion of obviousness. Rejections on obviousness cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; there must be some articulated reasoning with some rational underpinning to support the legal conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must clearly explain the reasons why a claimed invention would have been obvious in view of the prior art. Cite In re Kahn and KSR: provide explicit reasoning, not bare conclusions. Where a rationale is invoked, map factual findings to the rationale and legal standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability and reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: One of ordinary skill would have recognized that the results of the combination or substitution were predictable, and there was a reasonable expectation of success where required (e.g., 'obvious to try' contexts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predictability may be about (a) physical combinability and (b) that the combination would work for its intended purpose. If results would not have been predictable, the rationale cannot support obviousness. Examples: Adams and Crocs (nonobvious where predictable results not shown or prior art taught away); DePuy Spine: predictability must include working for intended purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching away reduces weight of obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: When the prior art teaches away from combining certain known elements or from the claimed modification, discovery of a successful combination may be nonobvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If references discourage the very combination or modification proposed, that can support nonobviousness (Adams, Crocs, DePuy Spine). Examiners must identify teachings that would have deterred a person of ordinary skill from combining the elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous prior art and reasonable pertinence
rubrics_metrics.description: References must be analogous art or reasonably pertinent to the particular problem with which the inventor was involved; KSR directs construing the scope of analogous art broadly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether a reference is in the same field of endeavor or is reasonably pertinent to the problem addressed. Even if in a different field, a reference may be relevant if it addresses a similar problem or would have been reasonably pertinent to one skilled in the art (see Wyers, ICON, and related examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulated reason or motivation to combine (including common sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: It can be important to identify a reason that would have prompted a person of ordinary skill in the relevant field to combine the elements in the way the claimed invention does; KSR allows recourse to logic, judgment, and common sense, but the analysis should explain why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation may derive from prior art teachings, market forces, or common sense, but examiners must explain the rationale. Common sense may support a motivation to combine in appropriate cases but must be accompanied by an explanation tied to the facts (see Wyers, Ecolab).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of optimization within ordinary skill
rubrics_metrics.description: If optimization of parameters or adjustment of application parameters would have been within the level of ordinary skill in the art, then combining or selecting those parameters may be obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a reference suggests a parameter and persons skilled could optimize it using routine experimentation, an obviousness rejection may be proper (Ecolab). Examiners should assess whether parameter optimization was within ordinary skill and whether a reasonable expectation of success existed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of a previously unknown problem can support nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee discovered a problem not recognized in the prior art, a modification to address that problem may have been nonobvious because there would have been no reason to incur additional expense or effort to make the modification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Omeprazole as an example: even if modifications were technologically possible, absence of recognition of the prior-art problem means no reason to modify, supporting nonobviousness. Examiners should look for evidence whether a problem was known or recognized in the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictable results require retention of prior-art functions
rubrics_metrics.description: A hallmark of a proper obviousness rejection based on combining known prior art elements is that one of ordinary skill would have expected the elements to maintain their respective properties or functions after combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the combination preserves each element's known properties/functions and yields predictable results, it supports obviousness (Sundance example). If the combination yields more than predictable results (an unexpected advantage), that supports nonobviousness (Crocs).
